newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Turkish military chief arrives in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Turkish military chief arrives in Cyprus.

text.p: Turkey's armed forces chief, Gen. Ismail Hakki Karadayi, arrived in northern Cyprus on Monday amid a row over the planned Greek Cypriot deployment of anti-aircraft missiles on the divided island.
Karadayi said the intended purchase of Russian-made S-300 missiles, which Turkey has threatened to knock out, was the latest in a Greek Cypriot armament campaign aimed against Turkey.
"I see the Greek Cypriot decision to buy the S-300 missiles as the culmination of provocation and over-militarisation," he said.
"Let no one forget what the real purpose is," he told reporters at Ercan airport in the Turkish Cypriot sector.
Turkey says the missiles would have an offensive aim because they could hit planes inside Turkish airspace. Cyprus is 80 km (50 miles) from the Turkish mainland.
"You cannot show a weapon that has a range of 150 to 160 km (93 to 100 miles) as a defensive system. This is not acceptable and it cannot be taken lightly," Karadayi said.

The Greek Cypriot administration, recognised internationally as the island's only government, says it needs the S-300s to counter any Turkish air strike. Turkey has kept 30,000 troops in Cyprus since it invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup attempt.
Karadayi, who has strong influence over Turkish policy, later held talks with Rauf Denktash, leader of a breakaway state in the north recognised only by Turkey.
The Cypriot government on Monday allayed fears of imminent conflict with Turkey but vowed to proceed with the missile deployment.

"What is needed right now is the concentration on efforts for a political solution to the Cyprus problem," spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides said after U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh met Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.
The U.S. envoy was to cross the U.N.-patrolled "Green Line" dividing Nicosia and the island to hold talks with Denktash later in the day.
